title: ⭐⭐ Revision: the grid, the crowd and the silent letters

questions.prompt: Six moments of one day at an on-line high school. The clues are not given in the order things happen: lunch begins an hour and a half after the break; the last class begins an hour after lunch; the break begins an hour after classes start; the pupils log on at nine and chat in what the timetable calls the school hall; Lesson 2 begins half an hour after the break; classes start half an hour after the pupils log on. Put the six moments in the order in which they happen.

options.text: the pupils log on and chat in the school hall
classes start
the break
Lesson 2
lunch
the last class

questions.explanation: Only one clue gives a time on the clock, so that is where the chain has to be fastened: the connection at nine. Half an hour later the classes begin, an hour after that comes the pause, and the whole grid can then be rebuilt from the pause, because two clues hang from it. The trap is exactly there. One of them adds half an hour and the other an hour and a half, so the meal is a full hour later than the class it looks as though it should precede, and a reader who takes the clues in the order they are printed puts the two the wrong way round. Work the six times out - nine, half past nine, half past ten, eleven, twelve and one o'clock - and the day falls into place on its own, one moment an hour or a half hour after the one before it.

questions.prompt: A matching exercise prints five words on the left, bullying, log on, appeal, texting and bustle, and six definitions on the right, one of which belongs to no word at all. The six are: writing on the computer; a crowd of people moving about in a busy way; testing; connecting a computer to a system; what makes something attractive; frightening or hurting a weaker person. A pupil has matched four of the words and has two definitions left over, testing and what makes something attractive, with only the word appeal still to place. What should he do?

options.text: take what makes something attractive, and leave testing matched to nothing
take testing, and leave what makes something attractive matched to nothing
take both definitions, since appeal is used in two senses in this lesson
go back and match testing to bustle, which he had placed too quickly

questions.explanation: The exercise warns you that a definition is left over, and this is the moment it was designed for: a pupil who has come this far by elimination will hand the last word whichever definition is nearest. So stop eliminating and read. Here the word is the one that names the pull a thing has on people, and one of the two lines still on the table says exactly that. The other names an activity that has nothing to do with drawing anybody anywhere, and it is meant to be left unmatched at the end: an unused definition is the expected result, not a sign that something has gone wrong. Nothing gives one word two definitions either. And the pair he is tempted to undo was right the first time: pulling a correct pair apart to make room for a definition that fits nothing is how a pupil turns four right answers into two wrong ones.

questions.prompt: In a role play, one student has just argued that a bullied child is safer working at home. The other student answers, in his own words: "He would certainly be safer from the bullies, but he would then spend five hours alone in a chair." What has he done in that single sentence?

options.text: he has granted the point and then argued against it all the same
he has agreed with it and given up his own side of the argument
he has refused the point flatly, without granting anything
he has asked for the point to be explained to him again

questions.explanation: Everything turns on the small word that sits in the middle of his answer. In front of it he hands his opponent something real, and he hands it in his own words: the child would indeed be safer from the bullies, and he says so before saying anything else. Behind it he sets his own objection, which is the sentence he came to say. That is the whole move: concede the true half, then attack what is left, and you have answered an argument instead of merely repeating that you disagree. He has not given up anything, since his objection follows immediately. He has not refused outright either, because a flat refusal keeps nothing of what the other said. And he asks for nothing: no question has been put, only a fact laid beside a fact.

questions.prompt: Four words of this lesson: right, taught, through, knee. In three of them the letters that are written and never sounded are the same pair. Which word does not share that pair?

options.text: the word knee
the word right
the word taught
the word through

questions.explanation: Three of these belong to one large family of English spellings, the one that keeps a g and an h side by side and pronounces neither: you hear nothing of them in what is correct, in what was learnt, or in going from one end of something to the other. The odd word out belongs to a different family, the one that opens on a k nobody says - the same family as knowledge and knife - and the letters it hides are neither the same pair nor in the same place, since its silent letter stands at the very front while the others bury theirs in the middle.

questions.prompt: A doctor tells a pupil who spends five hours a day in front of a screen that he will end up with a stiff back and tired eyes. The report calls these side-effects. What does that word name?

options.text: effects nobody wanted, that come along with a benefit
effects that show themselves on one side of the body only
effects the school produces on purpose and warns its pupils of
effects that appear long after a pupil has left the school

questions.explanation: Nobody opens a school in order to give children a stiff back. The teaching is what the day is for, and the aching body arrives with it, uninvited and unavoidable: that is the whole idea the word carries, and it is why this one line can be set against a long list of benefits without cancelling any of them. The side in it has nothing to do with left or right, so a symptom confined to half a body is a reading of the spelling and not of the word. Nothing about it is intended, which rules out anything a school does on purpose. And it names what happens while the thing is being used, not what turns up years later.

questions.prompt: A report closes by saying that the students who enrol in these schools do feel better, because they no longer suffer from bullying or from the bustling of a crowded school; that they are more confident; and that all they have to do is log on and start texting. What reason does the paragraph give for their feeling better?

options.text: two things that used to happen to them have stopped
their lessons have become easier to follow than before
they have far less writing to do than they used to
their teachers have stopped being strict with them

questions.explanation: Follow the word because and it points at a pair, not at a single cause: the deliberate cruelty of one child towards another, and the sheer press of bodies in a corridor, which is nobody's fault and wears nobody down on purpose. Both have stopped, and the closing lines hang the feeling better on that stopping and on nothing else. Read the sentence after it with the same care: the pupils are said to be more confident, but that is a second statement set beside the first, not a second thing the because reaches - a report may print two facts in a row without making one the cause of the other. Nothing in these lines touches the difficulty of the work, and the pupils are not writing less either, since the paragraph ends on them starting to write. As for a teacher's severity, it drove one pupil out of her old school, but it is not what these lines credit.
